transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-07-28 15:00 PDT | Duration: 45m
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Morales (Redwood SE), Maya Li (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (NovaPayments Head of ML), Tom Redding (Infra Lead), Priya Sharma (PM), Ben Ortiz (SRE)

Summary (auto): Reviewed POC metrics for Dedicated cluster sizing, discussed autoscaling policies and burst planning. Agreed to run burst test and for Redwood to send updated sizing with headroom.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Sofia): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — sizing recap, burst planning, autoscale policy choices, next steps. can everyone hear me?
00:06 Speaker 2 (Aisha): yes, loud and clear. thanks.
00:15 Speaker 1 (Sofia): great. Ethan, do you want to get us started with the numbers from last week's pilot?
00:20 Speaker 3 (Ethan): yeah, sure. so from the pilot we saw median token-per-request at about 320 tokens, average latency at p95 ~ 230ms on the dedicated G4x2 nodes when we batched at 16. the throughput peaked at 42 rps sustained for about 10 minutes during the midday surge. there was a short spike to 120 rps for maybe 20 seconds during the test traffic.
00:45 Speaker 4 (Aisha): that 120 spike is basically a marketing campaign burst, we see that on launch windows. our concern is that when that happens we hit higher latencies and perceived errors.
00:55 Speaker 3 (Ethan): right, and to add — the KV cache behavior also affected tail latency, the cache warmup after an idle period caused a couple hundred ms extra for the first few requests.
01:10 Speaker 5 (Tom): when you say KV cache, do you mean your prefix cache, or some other kv? we've got some microservices that chatter and keep connections warm, but our load balancer has a long idle timeout.
01:20 Speaker 3 (Ethan): yes prefix/K V cache — sometimes transcribed as K V catch in notes — it’s the per-model kv cache for key/value attention states. warming it helps, but doesn't fully mitigate a sudden 3x rps spike.
01:40 Speaker 1 (Sofia): ok so the question is — Dedicated sizing: do we size for peak, or do we rely on autoscaling + burst capacity? what are the pros/cons?
01:50 Speaker 6 (Priya): from product, we want predictable p95 under 300ms during business hours. marketing can tolerate slightly higher outside business hours, but not at launch windows.
02:05 Speaker 3 (Ethan): our recommendation for this POC is to configure a baseline Dedicated GPU pool sized for 50 rps sustained — that matches your 95th normal day traffic — plus a burst pool that can spin up additional instances. the tricky part is the spin-up time for GPUs and the model cold-start overhead, so we suggested a warm standby of N smaller instances that can handle short spikes while the larger instances come online.
02:30 Speaker 5 (Tom): what instance types again? you recommended the N16 profiles? our infra people prefer more modest instances for steady traffic and a couple of beefy ones for large batches.
02:42 Speaker 3 (Ethan): in the spreadsheet we put a mix: 4 x M60-equivalent for baseline (for cost reasons) and 2 x V100-equivalent as burst targets for heavy generation. we can also use quantized model variants on the smaller instances to reduce memory and warm-up times.
02:58 Speaker 4 (Aisha): can you explain the autoscale policy options in Redwood — like threshold-based vs predictive? we want something that won't thrash.
03:10 Speaker 3 (Ethan): sure. threshold-based uses queue length and CPU/GPU utilization with a cooldown window, e.g., scale out when avg GPU util > 65% for 30s, scale in after util < 40% for 3 minutes. predictive uses short-term traffic forecasting based on historical patterns — it can pre-scale for expected marketing spikes but needs reliable historical signals to avoid overprovisioning.
03:34 Speaker 5 (Tom): cooldowns are key. our infra team hates rapid scale-up/down and the networking churn. what's Redwood's recommended cooldown?
03:44 Speaker 3 (Ethan): we typically recommend a conservative cooldown: scale out cooldown 30–60s, scale in cooldown 180–300s for GPU-backed services. plus a pre-warming window for model weights if using full-size instances.
04:05 Speaker 4 (Aisha): about costs — do you have an estimate if we keep a standby warm pool vs having instant scale from hosted burst?
04:14 Speaker 1 (Sofia): yes, per the sizing sheet, keeping a 2-node warm standby adds roughly 18% to baseline monthly cost but reduces the p95 tail by ~35% during spikes. relying purely on spin-up reduced cost but our tests showed up to 700ms extra tail latency during cold starts.
04:35 Speaker 6 (Priya): can we do a hybrid: keep a small warm quantized variant that can serve 80 rps but at slightly lower quality, and then failover to full-size models when capacity is available?
04:47 Speaker 3 (Ethan): absolutely, that's the model-variant fallback pattern we recommend — smaller quantized model for immediate response, then redirect to high-quality model for background re-generation if necessary. we include quality monitoring and regression alerts so you can measure user impact.
05:10 Speaker 5 (Tom): how do we orchestrate fallback — is that in the Redwood router or in our app?
05:18 Speaker 3 (Ethan): Redwood can do routing rules at the platform level — route by policy (latency, cost, region). you can set automatic fallback when latency > X or when queue length > Y. alternatively some customers prefer app-level logic; both supported.
05:32 Speaker 4 (Aisha): what's the plan for the upcoming load test? we wanted to simulate the 120 rps 20s spike and a longer 5-minute campaign.
05:40 Speaker 1 (Sofia): yes, we propose two runs: short burst (120 rps for 30s) and sustained campaign (80 rps for 10 minutes). Ethan and Ben will coordinate the runbook. we should capture p50/p95/p99, queue lengths, scale events, and cold-start counts.
06:00 Speaker 7 (Ben): I'll need a runbook, access to the sizing spreadsheet, and the traffic generator config. scope network egress limits and auth tokens.
06:10 Speaker 3 (Ethan): I'll prepare the runbook and share a link to the harness. (link to runbook and sizing sheet shared: https://drive.company/sizing-novapay-2025-07-28.xlsx, runbook: https://drive.company/novapay-burst-runbook.md)
06:25 Speaker 4 (Aisha): one more question on monitoring: will we get token-level cost breakdowns in the console during the run?
06:32 Speaker 1 (Sofia): yes, Redwood Console will show token-level cost and latency bands per route. we'll also enable tracing for the test so you can map requests to scale events.
06:45 Speaker 5 (Tom): do you support SSO and audit logs for Dedicated? procurement will want SOC2 evidence.
06:52 Speaker 1 (Sofia): yes, Dedicated supports SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs. we also have SOC 2 Type II and can share the compliance pack — I'll drop the security docs after this call.
07:05 Speaker 6 (Priya): timeline — if we agree to the sizing and run next week, when can we have a recommendation for production commit?
07:12 Speaker 3 (Ethan): after the runs and spreadsheet updates, we can finalize recommended Dedicated commit sizes within 5 business days. procurement and legal time will vary.
07:25 Speaker 4 (Aisha): ok, last thing — what about region failover for capacity? if us-west saturates, can we burst into eu-west temporarily?
07:34 Speaker 3 (Ethan): yes, cross-region burst is supported but adds egress latency. we can set policies to prefer local region first, then overflow to secondary region. it's best for non-latency-critical background jobs. for user-facing realtime, we'd rather keep regional routing.
07:50 Speaker 1 (Sofia): perfect. recap: Redwood will update sizing sheet with 20% burst headroom and recommended cooldowns; Ethan to prepare runbook; Aisha to upload production week traces; run scheduled week of 2025-08-04.
08:05 Speaker 4 (Aisha): sounds good, thanks everyone.
08:12 Speaker 1 (Sofia): thanks all — we'll follow up in email with the links and action items.
